name: Water-Blob Impact
question: How do impact speed and size change the splash?
blurb: A round parcel of water falls into a pool and throws up a crown-like sheet and a central jet. This is a two-dimensional blob impact without surface tension, not a resolved droplet splash.
physics:
This exhibit runs six free-surface scenes from one solver — pick from the 'Scene' control: a dam break, a block dropped into a pool, a sloshing tank, pouring water into a glass, a wavemaker driving an ocean of waves, and a rigid ship floating on those waves. Each scene exposes its own controls (drop size and release height, slosh strength and period, spout width and pour speed, wavemaker stroke and period, ship size), so you can dial in the physics that matters for that scenario.

Take the dam break: hold back a column of water with a wall, remove the wall instantly, and gravity converts the column's potential energy into a fast horizontal surge. The front races along the floor, climbs the opposite wall, and overturns into a breaking jet. The free surface — the moving air–water boundary — folds over on itself, exactly the kind of large deformation and topology change that is painful for grid-based methods.

Smoothed-Particle Hydrodynamics takes a completely different, mesh-free view: the fluid is represented by a cloud of particles that carry mass and velocity and move with the flow (a Lagrangian description). Any continuous field — density, pressure, their gradients — is reconstructed at a particle by a smoothed, weighted sum over its neighbours within a smoothing length, using a bell-shaped kernel W. Because the particles simply follow the water, the free surface is wherever the particles happen to be — no interface tracking required.

Pressure is obtained from a stiff equation of state (weakly-compressible SPH): the fluid is treated as very slightly compressible so that small density changes produce the large pressures that resist compression. SPH is widely used for violent free-surface flows in coastal, marine and flood engineering.
terms:
• vi — velocity of particle i; Dvi/Dt is its acceleration following the flow
• mj — mass of neighbour particle j
• pi, pj — pressures (from the Tait equation of state); ρi, ρj — densities
• ∇Wij — gradient of the smoothing kernel between particles i and j; it carries the pressure force along the line joining them
• Πij — Monaghan artificial viscosity, added for stability at shocks/impacts
• g — gravity, the driving body force
• the walls are dynamic boundary particles: a fixed layer that feels the fluid pressure through the same equation of state and pushes back — a physical wall, not a penalty force, so the water near the walls behaves like the bulk
numerics: Weakly-compressible SPH: each particle carries mass and velocity; density and forces are smoothed sums over neighbours using a cubic-spline kernel. Pressure follows a stiff Tait equation of state (clamped ≥ 0 to avoid the free-surface tensile instability), with Monaghan artificial viscosity and a uniform background grid for fast neighbour search. The walls are dynamic boundary particles — fixed layers of particles that develop pressure through the same equation of state when the fluid presses on them, so the wall pushes back with real pressure (no penalty force on the fluid, no spurious near-wall motion); the wavemaker is simply a wall layer that moves. A δ-SPH density-diffusion term and XSPH velocity smoothing damp the acoustic noise and relax the initial lattice; the floating hull is a rigid body driven by contact forces from the fluid, gravity and damping, with limits on its motion.
ic: A body of water at rest under gravity — a tall column (dam break), a falling blob (droplet), a filled tank (slosh), a partly-filled glass (pour) or a wave train.
bc: Tank walls of fixed boundary particles (dynamic boundary condition); a free surface open to the air; the wavemaker is a moving wall layer; the ship scene adds a rigid hull driven by contact forces, gravity and damping, with limits on its motion.
validation: Qualitative demonstration: no surface tension, 2-D, weakly compressible.

params.name: scene
params.label: Scene
params.help: Which free-surface scenario to run. Each scene exposes its own controls below. Still water is the hydrostatic baseline: nothing should move.

params.name: width
params.label: Dam width
params.help: Width of the held-back water column (tank 5 × 3.2 m).

params.name: height
params.label: Dam height
params.help: Height of the column — more head → a faster, taller surge.

params.name: dropsize
params.label: Blob diameter
params.help: Diameter of the falling water blob (a parcel of water, not a capillary droplet — there is no surface tension in this model).

params.name: dropheight
params.label: Release height
params.help: How high the blob starts, as a fraction of tank height (sets the impact speed √(2 g h)).

params.name: sloshA
params.label: Slosh strength
params.help: Amplitude of the oscillating sideways gravity, as a multiple of g.

params.name: sloshT
params.label: Slosh period
params.help: Period of the side-to-side forcing. Near the tank's natural period the wave resonates and breaks.

params.name: spout
params.label: Spout width
params.help: Half-width of the pour stream as a fraction of the glass width. Values below 3 particle spacings are raised to that minimum (shown in derived quantities).

params.name: pourv
params.label: Pour speed
params.help: Speed the water leaves the spout. Faster → more splashing on impact.

params.name: waveA
params.label: Wavemaker stroke
params.help: Stroke of the wavemaker paddle (the wall's travel), which sets the wave amplitude indirectly — it is not the wave height itself. 0 = still paddle (free decay / equilibrium test for the ship).

params.name: waveT
params.label: Wave period
params.help: Period of the wavemaker — sets the wavelength of the train.

params.name: shipsz
params.label: Ship size
params.help: Scale of the floating hull. Bigger ships sit deeper and roll slower.

params.name: particles
params.label: Particles (≈)
params.help: Approximate number of SPH particles: sets the particle spacing dp (see derived quantities). More → finer splash, slower. The pour scene emits particles continuously and ignores this.

params.name: duration
params.label: Duration (×)
params.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
